vtrmc-1988-01.title: The parallelogram is a rhombus
vtrmc-1988-01.body:
Let $S=ABDE$ with the circle $C$ (center $O$) tangent to the sides $EA,AB,BD,DE$ at $P,Q,R,T$, and $\angle AED=\theta$.

*$S$ is a rhombus.* Tangent segments from a point to a circle are equal: $EP=ET$, $AP=AQ$, $BQ=BR$, $DR=DT$. Adding,
$$EA+BD=AB+DE .$$
In a parallelogram $EA=BD$ and $AB=DE$, so $2EA=2AB$: all four sides are equal.

*Area.* The distance between the parallel lines $AB$ and $ED$ is the diameter $2r$ (both are tangent to $C$). The side length $s$ satisfies $s\sin\theta=2r$ (height on side $ED$ from $A$). Hence
$$\text{Area}(S)=s\cdot2r=\frac{4r^2}{\sin\theta}.$$

Equivalently (the official form): in the rhombus $O$ is the intersection of the diagonals, $\angle EOD=\frac\pi2$, $\angle OED=\frac\theta2$, and $ED=ET+TD=r\cot\frac\theta2+r\tan\frac\theta2$, so the area is $4\cdot\frac12\cdot ED\cdot r=2r^2\left(\cot\frac\theta2+\tan\frac\theta2\right)$, which equals $\frac{2r^2}{\sin\frac\theta2\cos\frac\theta2}=\frac{4r^2}{\sin\theta}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{4r^2}{\sin\theta}$.**

vtrmc-1988-01.title: Area as sum of four triangles
vtrmc-1988-01.body:
Join $O$ to the four vertices. This splits $S$ into four triangles whose heights from $O$ all equal $r$ (the circle is tangent to every side). So
$$\text{Area}(S)=\tfrac12 r\,(\text{perimeter})=r\,(AB+AE).$$
On the other hand $\text{Area}(S)=AB\cdot2r$ (base $AB$, height $2r$ between the tangent lines $AB$ and $ED$), and likewise $=AE\cdot2r$. Comparing, $AB=AE=s$, and $\text{Area}=s\cdot s\sin\theta=2rs$, so $s=\frac{2r}{\sin\theta}$ and
$$\text{Area}(S)=\frac{4r^2}{\sin\theta}.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{4r^2}{\sin\theta}$.**

vtrmc-1988-02.title: Set up a linear Diophantine equation
vtrmc-1988-02.body:
Let the check be for $x$ dollars and $y$ cents, $0\le x,y\le99$ integers, i.e. $100x+y$ cents. He received $100y+x$ cents, so
$$100y+x-5=2(100x+y)\iff 98y=199x+5 .$$
Reducing modulo $98$: $199x+5\equiv3x+5\equiv0\pmod{98}$, i.e. $3x\equiv93\pmod{98}$. Since $\gcd(3,98)=1$, $x\equiv31\pmod{98}$, and with $0\le x\le99$ the only option is $x=31$. Then
$$y=\frac{199\cdot31+5}{98}=\frac{6174}{98}=63 .$$
Check: he got 63.31 dollars, spent 0.05, leaving 63.26 dollars $=2\times31.63$. ✓

The solution is unique: **the check was for 31.63 dollars.**

vtrmc-1988-02.title: Bound and search
vtrmc-1988-02.body:
From $98y=199x+5$ and $y\le99$: $199x\le98\cdot99-5$, so $x\le48$; also $199x+5$ must be divisible by $98$, and $199x+5=2\cdot98x+(3x+5)$, so $98\mid3x+5$. With $x\le48$, $3x+5\le149$, so $3x+5=98$, giving $x=31$, $y=2x+\frac{3x+5}{98}=62+1=63$.

**Answer: 31.63 dollars** (the only solution).

vtrmc-1988-03.title: Convert to a differential equation
vtrmc-1988-03.body:
Assume $y$ is continuous (so that the integral makes sense and is differentiable). Then $y(x)=x^2-\int_1^xy$ is differentiable, and differentiating,
$$y'+y=2x .$$
Also, putting $x=1$ in the equation gives $y(1)=1$.

The linear equation has integrating factor $e^x$: $(e^xy)'=2xe^x$, so $e^xy=2(x-1)e^x+C$ and
$$y=2x-2+Ce^{-x}.$$
From $y(1)=1$: $0+Ce^{-1}=1$, so $C=e$, and
$$y(x)=2x-2+e^{1-x}.$$
Conversely this function satisfies the original equation:
$$\int_1^x\big(2t-2+e^{1-t}\big)dt=(x-1)^2+1-e^{1-x},$$
and $2x-2+e^{1-x}+(x-1)^2+1-e^{1-x}=x^2$. ✓

So the "general solution" contains no arbitrary constant: the unique solution is $y=2x-2+e^{1-x}$.

vtrmc-1988-03.title: Undetermined coefficients
vtrmc-1988-03.body:
Try $y=Ax+B+Ce^{-x}$. Then
$$y+\int_1^xy\,dt=Ax+B+Ce^{-x}+\tfrac A2(x^2-1)+B(x-1)+C(e^{-1}-e^{-x})=\tfrac A2x^2+(A+B)x+\big(B-\tfrac A2-B+Ce^{-1}\big).$$
Matching with $x^2$: $\frac A2=1$, $A+B=0$, $-\frac A2+Ce^{-1}=0$, so $A=2$, $B=-2$, $C=e$, giving $y=2x-2+e^{1-x}$. Uniqueness: if $y_1,y_2$ are continuous solutions, $w=y_1-y_2$ satisfies $w+\int_1^xw=0$, hence $w'=-w$, $w(1)=0$, so $w\equiv0$.

vtrmc-1988-04.title: Reduce modulo $a^{n+1}+1$
vtrmc-1988-04.body:
We need $a^{n+1}+1\mid a^2+a^{2n}$.

**$a=1$:** $a^2+b^2=2=ab+1$, so every $n$ works.

**$a\ge2$.** Since $a^{n-1}(a^{n+1}+1)=a^{2n}+a^{n-1}$,
$$a^2+a^{2n}=a^{n-1}(a^{n+1}+1)+\big(a^2-a^{n-1}\big),$$
so the condition is equivalent to
$$a^{n+1}+1\ \big|\ a^2-a^{n-1}.$$
- If $n=3$, then $a^2-a^{n-1}=0$, which is divisible. Indeed $a^2+a^6=a^2(a^4+1)$.
- If $n\ne3$, then $a^{n-1}\ne a^2$, so $a^2-a^{n-1}\ne0$, and
$$|a^2-a^{n-1}|<\max(a^2,a^{n-1})<a^{n+1}+1$$
(for $n=1,2$ the maximum is $a^2<a^{n+1}+1$; for $n\ge4$ it is $a^{n-1}<a^{n+1}$). A nonzero integer of smaller absolute value is not divisible by $a^{n+1}+1$.

**Answer: for $a=1$ all $n\ge1$; for $a\ge2$ exactly $n=3$.** ∎

vtrmc-1988-04.title: Official-style argument
vtrmc-1988-04.body:
For $a\ge2$ suppose $a^{n+1}+1\mid a^2+a^{2n}$.

- $n=1$: $a^2+1\mid2a^2=2(a^2+1)-2$, so $a^2+1\mid2$, impossible for $a\ge2$.
- $n=2$: $a^3+1\mid a^2+a^4=a(a^3+1)+(a^2-a)$, so $a^3+1\mid a^2-a$, impossible since $0<a^2-a<a^3+1$.
- $n=3$: $a^4+1\mid a^2+a^6=a^2(a^4+1)$ — works.
- $n\ge4$: $a^{n+1}+1$ divides $a^{2n}+a^2-a^{n-1}(a^{n+1}+1)=a^2-a^{n-1}$, a negative number with $|a^2-a^{n-1}|<a^{n-1}<a^{n+1}+1$ — impossible.

So $n=3$ is the only solution when $a>1$, and every $n$ works when $a=1$. ∎

vtrmc-1988-05.title: Mean value theorem
vtrmc-1988-05.body:
By the mean value theorem there is $\xi$ between $\alpha$ and $x_0$ with
$$0.0001=|f(\alpha)-f(x_0)|=|f'(\xi)|\,|\alpha-x_0|\ge2|\alpha-x_0| ,$$
so $|\alpha-x_0|\le0.00005$ for every such $f$.

The bound is attained: take $\alpha=\tfrac12$, $x_0=\tfrac12-0.00005$ and $f(x)=2(x-\tfrac12)$. Then $|f'|=2$, $f(\alpha)=0$, $f(x_0)=-0.0001$, and $|\alpha-x_0|=0.00005$.

So the smallest upper bound is $0.00005=5\times10^{-5}$.

vtrmc-1988-05.title: Monotonicity (official idea)
vtrmc-1988-05.body:
A derivative has the intermediate value property (Darboux), and $|f'|\ge2$ means $f'$ never takes values in $(-2,2)$; so either $f'\ge2$ everywhere or $f'\le-2$ everywhere. Say $f'\ge2$ (the other case is symmetric). Then $f$ is increasing and, for $x_0<\alpha$,
$$f(\alpha)-f(x_0)=\int_{x_0}^{\alpha}f'\ \ge\ 2(\alpha-x_0)\quad(\text{or use the MVT}),$$
i.e. $0.0001\ge2(\alpha-x_0)$. Hence $|\alpha-x_0|\le0.00005$, with equality for a linear $f$ of slope $\pm2$.

**Answer: $0.00005$.**

vtrmc-1988-06.title: Interior critical points and endpoints
vtrmc-1988-06.body:
On $[-1,1]$ the function $f(x)=ax-bx^3$ ($a,b>0$) has at most two interior critical points, $x=\pm s$ with $s=\sqrt{\frac{a}{3b}}$, so four extrema means: the two endpoints $\pm1$ and the two interior points $\pm s$, $0<s<1$. Since $f$ is odd, it suffices to require $|f(s)|=1$ and $|f(1)|=1$.

At $x=s$: $f(s)=as-bs^3=as-\frac a3s=\frac{2a}{3}s$, so $f(s)=1$ gives $a=\frac{3}{2s}$ and then $b=\frac{a}{3s^2}=\frac{1}{2s^3}$.

At $x=1$: $f(1)=a-b=\frac{3}{2s}-\frac1{2s^3}=\frac{3s^2-1}{2s^3}$.
- $f(1)=1$: $2s^3-3s^2+1=0\iff(s-1)^2(2s+1)=0$, so $s=1$, which is not an interior point (then there are only two extrema).
- $f(1)=-1$: $2s^3+3s^2-1=0\iff(s+1)^2(2s-1)=0$, so $s=\frac12$.

Thus $s=\frac12$, $a=3$, $b=4$:
$$f(x)=3x-4x^3,\qquad f(\pm\tfrac12)=\pm1,\quad f(\pm1)=\mp1 .$$
Between these points $f$ is monotone, so $|f|\le1$ on $[-1,1]$ and the four points are genuine extrema (local maxima/minima of $f$ on the interval).

*Note.* The official solution sheet arrives at $|a-b|=1$ but then states "$a=.1$ and $b=1.1$", which does not work: for those values the interior extrema are only $\approx\pm0.0116$. The correct pair is $a=3$, $b=4$.

**Answer: $a=3$, $b=4$.**

vtrmc-1988-06.title: Chebyshev polynomial
vtrmc-1988-06.body:
The Chebyshev polynomial $T_3(x)=\cos(3\arccos x)=4x^3-3x$ satisfies $|T_3|\le1$ on $[-1,1]$ and attains $\pm1$ alternately at $x=\cos\frac{k\pi}3$, i.e. at $x=1,\frac12,-\frac12,-1$ — four points. Hence $f=-T_3=3x-4x^3$ has the required form with $a=3$, $b=4$.

Verification: $f'(x)=3-12x^2=0$ at $x=\pm\frac12$, $f(\frac12)=\frac32-\frac12=1$, $f(-\frac12)=-1$, $f(1)=-1$, $f(-1)=1$.

**Answer: $a=3$, $b=4$.**

vtrmc-1988-07.title: Cantor construction; inf and sup
vtrmc-1988-07.body:
**(a)** $f$ maps an interval $[p,q]\subseteq[0,1]$ to $[\frac p3,\frac q3]\cup[\frac{p+2}3,\frac{q+2}3]$, one copy in $[0,\frac13]$ and one in $[\frac23,1]$. So
$$f(I)=[0,\tfrac13]\cup[\tfrac23,1],\qquad f(f(I))=[0,\tfrac19]\cup[\tfrac29,\tfrac39]\cup[\tfrac69,\tfrac79]\cup[\tfrac89,1],$$
$$f(f(f(I)))=[0,\tfrac1{27}]\cup[\tfrac2{27},\tfrac3{27}]\cup[\tfrac6{27},\tfrac7{27}]\cup[\tfrac8{27},\tfrac9{27}]\cup[\tfrac{18}{27},\tfrac{19}{27}]\cup[\tfrac{20}{27},\tfrac{21}{27}]\cup[\tfrac{24}{27},\tfrac{25}{27}]\cup[\tfrac{26}{27},1].$$
The sketch: eight closed intervals of length $\frac1{27}$ on $[0,1]$ — remove the middle third of $[0,1]$, then the middle thirds of the two remaining pieces, then of the four remaining pieces (the third stage of the Cantor set).

**(b)** No. Let $T$ be bounded with $f(T)=T$; if $T=\varnothing$ it does not contain $\frac12$, so let $T\ne\varnothing$, $m=\inf T$, $M=\sup T$.

The maps $x\mapsto\frac x3$ and $x\mapsto\frac{x+2}3$ are increasing, so $\inf f(T)=\min\left(\frac m3,\frac{m+2}3\right)=\frac m3$ and $\sup f(T)=\max\left(\frac M3,\frac{M+2}3\right)=\frac{M+2}3$. From $f(T)=T$:
$$m=\frac m3\Rightarrow m=0,\qquad M=\frac{M+2}3\Rightarrow M=1 .$$
So $T\subseteq[0,1]$.

Suppose $\frac12\in T=f(T)$. Then $\frac12=\frac t3$ or $\frac12=\frac{t+2}3$ for some $t\in T$, i.e. $t=\frac32$ or $t=-\frac12$. Both lie outside $[0,1]$ — contradiction. Hence **$T$ cannot contain $\frac12$.** ∎

vtrmc-1988-07.title: Ternary digits
vtrmc-1988-07.body:
**(a)** In base $3$, $x\mapsto\frac x3$ prepends the digit $0$ and $x\mapsto\frac{x+2}3$ prepends the digit $2$ after the point. Hence $f^3(I)$ is the set of $x\in[0,1]$ having a ternary expansion $0.d_1d_2d_3\ldots$ with $d_1,d_2,d_3\in\{0,2\}$, i.e. the $8$ intervals $\left[\frac{k}{27},\frac{k+1}{27}\right]$ with $k=9d_1+3d_2+d_3\in\{0,2,6,8,18,20,24,26\}$ — the list above.

**(b)** As shown, $T\subseteq[0,1]$. Iterating $T=f(T)$, every $x\in T$ satisfies $x\in f^k(T)\subseteq f^k([0,1])$ for all $k$, so $x$ lies in the Cantor set (expansions with digits $0,2$ only). But $\frac12=0.1111\ldots_3$ has the unique ternary expansion with all digits $1$, so $\frac12\notin$ Cantor set, and $\frac12\notin T$. ∎

vtrmc-1988-08.title: A bijection
vtrmc-1988-08.body:
Represent a triangle by its side lengths $a\le b\le c$ (positive integers with $a+b>c$); incongruent triangles correspond to different triples.

*From perimeter $n-3$ to $n$.* If $(a,b,c)$ is a triangle with perimeter $n-3$, then $(a+1,b+1,c+1)$ has perimeter $n$, the order is preserved, and $(a+1)+(b+1)=a+b+2>c+1$. This map is injective.

*Surjective when $n$ is even.* Let $(a,b,c)$, $a\le b\le c$, be a triangle with perimeter $n$ even. Then $a+b-c=n-2c$ is even, and it is positive, so $a+b-c\ge2$. Consider $(a-1,b-1,c-1)$:
- $a-1\ge1$: from $a+b\ge c+2$ and $b\le c$ we get $a\ge2$;
- triangle inequality: $(a-1)+(b-1)=a+b-2\ge c>c-1$; the other inequalities ($a-1+c-1>b-1$ etc.) follow from $c\ge b\ge a$.

So $(a-1,b-1,c-1)$ is a triangle with perimeter $n-3$ that maps to $(a,b,c)$. Hence the map is a bijection and
$$T(n)=T(n-3)\qquad(n\text{ even}).$$
∎

(For odd $n$ it can fail: $T(7)=2$ (triangles $1,3,3$ and $2,2,3$) but $T(4)=0$; here $(1,3,3)$ has no preimage.)

vtrmc-1988-08.title: Check with a count
vtrmc-1988-08.body:
The bijection above is the proof; as a sanity check, list small cases with $a\le b\le c$:
- $n=6$: $(2,2,2)$ — $T(6)=1$; $n-3=3$: $(1,1,1)$ — $T(3)=1$.
- $n=8$: $(2,3,3)$ — $T(8)=1$; $T(5)=1$: $(1,2,2)$.
- $n=10$: $(2,4,4),(3,3,4)$ — $T(10)=2$; $T(7)=2$: $(1,3,3),(2,2,3)$.
- $n=12$: $(2,5,5),(3,4,5),(4,4,4)$ — $T(12)=3$; $T(9)=3$: $(1,4,4),(2,3,4),(3,3,3)$.

In each case subtracting $1$ from every side matches the lists exactly, as the proof predicts. A computer check confirms $T(n)=T(n-3)$ for all even $n$ up to $28$. ∎
